To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the interaction of mesenchmal stromal cells (MSKCs) with natural killer cells (NKs) is a dynamic process that can be modeled in vitro using poly(I:C) stimulated MSCs and NK cells, and that activated tissue-resident MSC regulate NK cell immune and tissue-regenerative functions.
activated tissue-resident MSC regulate natural killer cell function and tissue-regenerative function.
activated tissue-resident mesenchymal stem cells regulate natural killer cell immune function and tissue-regenerative properties.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how tissue-resident MSC populations are activated by infection and injury to promote immune and tissue regenerative responses, as well as how activated MSCs in turn regulate NK cell immune and tissue-regenerative function.
understanding the role of mesenchymale stromal cells in the context of innate and adaptive immunity, as well as tissue homeostasis.
the role of the innate immune system in the development of chronic diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study shows that the interaction between MSCs and NK cells is more complex than previously thought and that MSCs are not only able to inhibit NK cells but also to activate NK cell effector functions.
activated tissue-resident MSC can regulate natural killer cell immune and tissue-regenerative function in a time dependent manner.

the interaction of activated MSCs with NK cells results in the generation of regulatory senescent NK cells that limit the inflammatory response and promote survival, proliferation and pro-angiogenesis of the tissue-resident MSC population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown a time-dependent system whereby activated tissue-resident MSC secrete factors that enhance NK cell effectors function and regulate the inflammatory response, while at later times, the same factors limit the NK cell effector response and induce a regulatory senesent-like phenotype that provides feedback to MSCs.
tissue-resident mesenchymal cells can be activated by inflammatory signals, and in turn, regulate the function of innate immune cells.
we have identified a novel role for tissue-resident MSC in the regulation of NK cell immune function and tissue-regenerative capacity, and that this regulation occurs in a time-dependent manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tissue-resident MSC populations are not simply bystanders in innate immunity and tissue repair, but rather are active participants in regulating the innate immune and tissue repair response.
the interaction between MSCs and NK cells is not static and is dependent on the inflammatory context and the activation state of the cells.
the interaction of NK and MSCs is not a static interaction, but rather one that is dynamic and time-dependent.
